q: What is vipassana?
k: meaning definition insight meditation explain
a:
Vipassanā means seeing clearly. Seeing things as they really are.

Vipassana is not really a technique. It's the result. The technique is mindfulness, sati, practised according to the Buddha's four foundations of mindfulness, the Satipaṭṭhāna. Body, feelings, mind, and dhammas. We keep stepping back and seeing each thing as a thing: it arises, it stays a while, it passes. Not mine, not me, not myself.

When you see that clearly, boom, something lets go. That's vipassana.

q: What is meditation, really?
k: bhavana purpose why meditate training mind
a:
The Pāḷi word is bhāvanā. It means cultivation, developing the mind. Developing the skilful states: awareness, energy, concentration, confidence and wisdom.

Just like the gym trains the body, meditation trains the mind. It's not esoteric. Not about visions. We deal with the raw data: seeing, hearing, touching, thinking. And we learn not to be bullied by it.

q: How do I start meditating at home?
k: beginner begin first steps instructions home practice how to meditate
a:
Sit on a cushion or a chair, spine upright, eyes closed. Put your attention on the belly. When it rises, softly note in the mind: rising. When it falls: falling.

When the mind wanders, and it will, note: thinking, thinking. Then back to rising and falling. That's it. Note, know, let go.

Start with 20 minutes a day. Ten minutes of walking meditation before makes the sitting much better. Be kind to yourself. Listen to the tone you use when you catch yourself drifting.

q: What does "note, know, let go" mean?
k: formula noting knowing letting go labelling
a:
Three steps.

Note: activating awareness. You catch what's happening now. Rising. Hearing. Thinking.

Know: seeing it with wisdom. It's just a thing. Not mine, not me, not myself. A thought is there. A sound is there.

Let go: and back to the present moment.

Note, know, let go. Note, know, let go. Every second, if you can. When you get that going, the fog of what you thought was reality starts to crack. You break through to the present moment.

q: Is "rising, falling" a mantra?
k: repeat words label belly abdomen breath noting
a:
No. It's not a mantra. You can't say rising if there is no rising. It has to match what you actually feel.

Each rising has a beginning, a middle and an end. Each falling too. We try to nail each one. If there's a pause, wait. Like a sniper, not moving. Then the next rising comes, and you catch it.

The note is soft, a small part of your attention. Most of it is feeling the actual movement.

q: I keep controlling my breath when I watch it. What do I do?
k: control breathing stop breathing forcing subtle rising falling hard to find
a:
Very common. Controlling the breath is meditating with desire. That's not what we're doing.

What worked for me: stop, and wait. Don't do anything. Freeze, like a tree. The breath kicks in by itself. Then note: controlling, controlling. See it as a thing, not you. Then go back to rising and falling.

If you can't find the rising and falling at all, lie down for a moment and find it there. Then sit up and stay with it.

q: My mind keeps wandering. Am I doing it wrong?
k: thoughts thinking distracted cannot focus concentrate busy mind stop thinking
a:
No. Mind going astray is natural. You'll drift away a thousand times in a session. It doesn't matter how many.

You're not going to stop thinking. The mind will think forever. That's its nature. We learn not to sink into it. To wake up from the movie and see it's a movie.

Each time you notice, note it: thinking, thinking. Then back. That noticing is the practice. Like a pebble in your shoe: are you upset you found the pebble? No, it's good. Take it out and keep walking.

q: Should I finish a thought before I go back to the breath?
k: participate in thoughts follow thought drop thought
a:
Never. You don't participate.

One man on our Thailand retreat said in the sharing circle it was life-changing for him. He always thought he had to finish a thought before moving on. Discovering he could just drop it was a liberation.

As soon as you notice you're inside a thought, step out. Thinking. Boom. Back to your main object.

q: I keep falling asleep when I meditate. What can I do?
k: drowsy sleepy tired nodding off sloth torpor dull heavy after lunch
a:
Sloth and torpor. One of the five hindrances. You need to stir up energy.

Do longer, more energetic walking meditation, really on top of it: lifting, moving, placing. That energy carries into the sitting. Sit with the eyes open for a while. Stand up on your mat. Add more objects: rising, falling, sitting, touching.

In Thailand, before the afternoon sit, I used to splash cold water on my face and the back of my neck. Wet your hair. It helps.

q: My mind is too restless to sit. What should I do?
k: restlessness agitated anxious cannot sit still worry planning
a:
Note it. Restless, restless. Planning, planning. Don't fight it. It's not a disturbance; it's an object of meditation.

Slow, precise walking meditation helps a lot before you sit. And come back to the body again and again: rising, falling, sitting, touching.

Restlessness often has roots in the past, things we're not proud of. That's why the precepts matter. Virtue is your security. With a clean conscience, the mind settles much more easily.

q: How do I deal with knee or back pain while sitting?
k: pain hurt knees back legs numb sitting posture discomfort ache
a:
First, look after the body. Raise the hips on a cushion so the knees are lower. Try a bench or a chair. Yoga every morning helps.

Then, the meditation side. Pain is a concept. Go into the centre of the sensation. What's really there? Burning. Pressure. Twisting. Heat. Note that. And note the feeling: unpleasant, unpleasant. And the reaction: disliking.

You can keep rising and falling as your main object and add it: rising, falling, heat. Every retreat someone tells me: "I did it, and poof, it was gone." If it's chronic or an injury, change position mindfully and tell the teacher. That's wisdom, not weakness.
refs: Knee and back pain in meditation

q: Do I have to sit cross-legged?
k: lotus chair cushion bench kneel posture sitting position
a:
No. Cushion, bench, chair, all fine. Upright spine, relaxed.

Think of the cobra. Stretched out on the ground, the eagle can catch it. Coiled and upright, nobody can touch it. Upright, alert, but not rigid.
refs: Knee and back pain in meditation

q: Can I meditate lying down?
k: lie down bed tent supine lying meditation
a:
Yes. Lying-down meditation was very powerful for me on retreats. It gives continuity. Before sleep, after lunch, resting in your tent: rising, falling.

The danger is drifting into sleep or into muddle-minded thinking when nobody's looking. Balance on that edge: almost going, but still aware.

It's also a good way to find the rising and falling if you struggle with it sitting.

q: How do I do walking meditation?
k: walking meditation lifting moving placing steps technique
a:
Choose a straight path of 10 to 20 steps. Eyes looking at the ground a couple of metres ahead.

Start with left, right. Then slow down: lifting, placing. Then three parts: lifting, moving, placing. Note each one exactly as it happens.

At the end, stop: standing, standing. Hearing. Then intending to turn, turning. Intending to walk. And again.

Don't think it's just stretching the legs. Most people first experience the present moment in walking meditation.

q: Do I note rising and falling during walking meditation?
k: walking belly breath combine
a:
No. We don't do rising and falling in walking at all. Just lifting, moving, placing.

When you stop at the end of the path, you can note standing, and hearing. Hearing is a wonderful object to snap you back into the present. It's always there.

q: How do I deal with strong emotions like anger, sadness or depression?
k: emotion anger sad depression anxiety fear feelings overwhelmed grief
a:
Step out of it and see it as a thing. Sadness, sadness. Anger, anger. Fear.

"I am depressed." Who is depressed? If you learn this skill, you can step out and see the state as an object, not you. It only stays because you give it attention, because you take it personally. Push it away, and you're participating by aversion. Grab it, you're participating by craving.

Look under the bed with wisdom: no ghosts. Seen clearly, it arises, it stays a while, it passes.

If you're struggling with your mental health, please also get support from a professional. Meditation is a powerful tool, not a replacement for care.

q: Isn't it better to talk about my problems to release them?
k: therapy talking release trauma process story
a:
It's a common understanding: talk about it more and you release it. You might feel a bit lighter for a while. But often it stirs things up and brings them back to the surface, again and again.

From the Buddhist side, the issue exists as long as there is identification with it. In vipassana we step out of the content, the story, and see the structure: it's a thought, it's a memory, it's a feeling. The story isn't interesting anymore. There could be so many different stories. We're interested in seeing the thing as a thing.

If you're working with a therapist, that's good. These can support each other.

q: Noise disturbs my meditation. What do I do?
k: noise sound loud disturbance neighbours hearing
a:
Nothing is a disturbance to your meditation. Nothing.

Note it: hearing, hearing. Not "car" or "bird". Is it a bird singing or a motorbike revving? It doesn't really matter. Hearing is occurring.

I remember one retreat in Thailand: a man behind me with a noisy stomach, cracking joints every time he moved. Then a temple festival nearby with a Thai rock band. By the end, it was just hearing. No problem. I wasn't reacting.

q: How long should I meditate each day?
k: minutes duration daily time hour
a:
Choose something you can keep. Beginners: 15 to 20 minutes, once a day. More experienced: 45 minutes to an hour keeps the mind clear.

Better a little every day than a lot for two weeks and then nothing. It works like brushing your teeth. You don't brush really well for seven days and then stop for a month.
refs: Keeping your practice going at home

q: How do I keep practising after the retreat?
k: home daily routine habit maintain continue practice after retreat
a:
Make it non-negotiable, like brushing your teeth. You don't decide every morning whether to do it.

Two good times: early morning (everyone has time at 5am) and before sleep. The Buddha said falling asleep mindful, you sleep at ease and wake happily.

Throughout the day, come back for three minutes every hour or so. When you're waiting in a queue, meditate: rising, falling. Make a little corner at home. Read a little of the suttas to keep the mind afloat. And come back to a retreat once or twice a year.

q: Should I meditate before sleep?
k: night bedtime insomnia sleep better
a:
Yes. Don't go to sleep muddle-minded. The Buddha listed the drawbacks: you sleep badly, wake miserably, have bad dreams. Fall asleep mindful and aware, and you sleep at ease and wake happily.

Tidy up the mind at the end of the day like you'd tidy the kitchen. Lie down, rising, falling, until you're gone.

q: What is mettā, loving-kindness meditation?
k: metta loving kindness compassion kindness meditation
a:
Mettā is loving-kindness. Strictly it's a different meditation from vipassana: here we work with concepts, imagining people and wishing them well. But it complements vipassana beautifully. It keeps the practice soft, not too dry or tense.

Start with yourself: may I be happy, may I be peaceful, may I be free from suffering. Then someone who helped you. A friend. A neutral person. A difficult person. Then all beings.

We do it every evening on retreat, when the sun goes down.

q: How do I deal with difficult or aggressive people?
k: conflict aggressive bully enemy hate resentment forgive
a:
You never win by answering aggression with aggression. You win when you don't answer with the same.

Turn the mind to the opposite: loving-kindness. Holding resentment is like holding a hot coal; it burns you, not the other person. Freeze like a tree when anger comes, and let it pass.

Do mettā every day, especially for that person. See how it changes your life. Often the situation just removes itself.

And if you're in danger, get real help. Kindness doesn't mean staying unsafe.

q: Why is the teaching offered for donation (dāna)?
k: dana donation cost free generosity pay price money
a:
It's important for vipassana to be offered for donation, not to make private profit. It's the purest way.

For us teachers, it's service. There's great joy in giving this knowledge. For you, you meet the teaching without a consumer expectation. The organisational fee, £149 for the 7-day retreat, covers only food and camping. Everything beyond that is your choice. At the end, you decide what the experience was worth to you, and give in a way that doesn't devalue it.
refs: How much does a vipassana retreat cost?

q: Why is generosity important?
k: generosity giving dana prosperity selfishness abundance
a:
Generosity is giving away a chunk of selfishness. "It's mine." And then a piece of it, given to the whole. A beautiful state of mind.

If you're a cheapskate and don't have much money, you especially need to practise generosity. Sounds contrary, right? But this is the way. Dāna is the gateway to prosperity. The universe doesn't know the ratio. You give with a full heart, something meaningful for you, and it can come back a hundred times.

q: What should a lay person practise?
k: lay life householder daily life pillars precepts virtue
a:
Three pillars for lay life: virtuous behaviour, generosity and meditation.

Virtue is keeping the five precepts: not killing, not stealing, no sexual misconduct, not lying, no intoxicants. Generosity is dāna. Meditation is bhāvanā. Keep a little of all three every day, and they hold each other up.

q: What are the precepts and why do we keep them?
k: precepts sila virtue morality five precepts eight rules
a:
Five training rules for lay life: not killing, not taking what isn't given, no sexual misconduct, not lying, no intoxicants that cloud the mind. On retreat we take eight.

Without virtue, it's very hard to meditate. As mindfulness sharpens, you remember everything. If you've been hurting people, it comes up and the mind can't settle.

There is no security in the world out there. But in wholesome states of mind, there is security. Virtue is your security.

q: Why is not lying so important?
k: truth honesty right speech lie words
a:
Many years ago I took it as a vow: I'm not going to lie. Not easy sometimes. But if you take it seriously, your word becomes very powerful. You almost create reality with your word. What you say seems to start happening.

So you have to be careful with your words afterwards. They have power.

q: What does "mind is the forerunner" mean?
k: dhammapada verse 1 intention leader mind
a:
It's the first verse of the Dhammapada. "Intention is the leader of things; intention is first, they're made by intention." Act with a corrupt mind, and suffering follows you like the wheel follows the ox. Act with a clear mind, and happiness follows you like a shadow.

More clarity in your mind, more lovely people you meet. The world reflects the mind. That's why we train it.

q: What is the Buddha's teaching about suffering?
k: dukkha suffering four noble truths unhappiness
a:
The whole teaching is about lessening suffering. Unnecessary suffering.

So much of it we take on by taking things personally. The more you understand the nature of things, the less you need to take them personally. The more personally you take things, the more suffering there is.

Dukkha: unsatisfactory, sometimes translated as suffering. Everything conditioned is unstable, so holding on to it hurts. Like carrying a bag of cement that isn't even your bag. Ooh, my cement. Then you see it. And you drop it.

q: What are the three characteristics?
k: anicca dukkha anatta impermanence non-self three marks
a:
Three characteristics of all phenomena. Anicca, impermanence: everything arises and passes. Dukkha, unsatisfactoriness: nothing conditioned can fully satisfy. Anattā, non-self: it's not mine, not me, not myself. Also out of control.

You don't learn them from books. You see them in the thoughts, the sounds, the sensations. Come, stay, go. No owner. That's the doorway to insight.

q: What is Nibbāna?
k: nirvana nibbana enlightenment liberation awakening
a:
The original meaning of Nibbāna is the going out of a flame. Where did the flame go? To the heaven of flames? No. It just went out. When there are conditions, there's a candle and a flame. When there are no conditions, there's none of it.

An unconditioned state. Great peace. Release. The Buddha said the ocean has one taste, the taste of salt; his teaching has one taste, the taste of freedom.

q: How do I stop taking things personally?
k: ego identification self take personally let go
a:
That's the whole training. Until you're taking it personally, you won't be able to let it go.

Every time a thought, a feeling, a mood comes, step back. It's just a thing. A thought is there. Anger is there. Not mine, not me. Like a cloud: I'm not the cloud, it's passing.

The more you marinate yourself in a state, the more you become that person. If you marinate a pickle in salt, what will it taste like? Rather salty. So step out, and stop marinating.

q: I keep trying to get something from meditation. Is that a problem?
k: expectation trying striving achieve results goal effort
a:
Yes, this is the struggle, especially for successful people. Used to getting things. Check, check, plan. "In seven days I'm going to get it."

As long as you're there trying to get something, it's impossible. It's only when you're not there, lost in the technique, that it works. Remember when you were happiest? Lost in a good film, snowboarding, surfing. Not thinking about yourself.

Kill the meditator. Nobody is meditating here. Just rising, falling. Meditation is about letting go, not getting something else.

q: How is this different from a Goenka retreat?
k: goenka body scan difference compare tradition mahasi technique
a:
Same root: the Buddha's four foundations of mindfulness. Different method.

Goenka's tradition uses the breath at the nostrils, then systematic body scanning. We teach in the Mahasi Sayadaw tradition: rising and falling of the belly, mental noting, walking meditation with the same precision, and noting all four foundations through the day.

If you've done Goenka, that concentration will help. But during our retreat, put that technique aside and give this one full power. Riding two horses at once works only if you're a circus rider.

q: Can I mix different meditation techniques?
k: mix combine techniques breath nose switch
a:
Not during a retreat. It brings confusion very quickly. Any meditation only works when you give it full power. It doesn't work slippery.

When you notice the mind wants to go back to the old familiar technique, note it: wanting, wanting comfort. Then back to rising and falling. At home, later, practise what really works for you.

q: Can a beginner come on a silent retreat?
k: beginner first time never meditated can I come suitable
a:
Yes. Every group has first-timers. They often do very well because they come without expectations.

We teach everything from zero, step by step, adding one object each day. Sittings are 45 minutes, alternating with walking, and there's yoga every morning. If you can sit for about half an hour in some position and follow a schedule for a week, you can do it.

If you have a mental health condition, please tell us when you book so we can talk about it first.
refs: Can a beginner do a vipassana retreat?

q: Will the retreat be hard?
k: difficult hard tough challenge day two three struggle
a:
For a couple of days, yes. Adjust your expectations. You won't be sitting in lotus on a mountain top for the first two days.

The body complains, the mind negotiates. "Oh, your knee. You might just go and lie down." It always finds a fresh reason. This is normal, like gym soreness: it leads to adaptation and strength.

Around day three the body adjusts, the mind settles, and the real work starts. Towards the end, many people have more energy than in years. Don't get off the surgery table halfway.

q: Why do we keep silence on retreat?
k: noble silence talking speak why silent
a:
Silence is a gift, not a punishment. You don't have to be anybody for anyone. No small talk, no performing. All the energy that usually goes out through the mouth stays with the practice.

And it's easy to keep the precept of not lying when you're not talking at all.

You'll be surprised how nourishing it is when you don't have to speak to anyone. You can always talk to the teacher in your interview.

q: Where are the retreats and how do I get there?
k: location venue where hardwick oxfordshire travel train london directions

q: What should I bring to the retreat?
k: packing list bring tent sleeping bag clothes
a:
You camp, so: a tent (or rent one at booking), a warm sleeping bag and mat, a pillow, a head torch. Warm layers, a hat and gloves for 5am sits, waterproofs. Your own cutlery, plate, bowl and cup. A yoga mat and a blanket or shawl for sitting. Swimwear for the river and sauna.

Leave books, journals and work at home. Your phone stays off.

q: What food is served on retreat?
k: food meals vegan vegetarian diet ayurvedic
a:
Plant-based Ayurvedic meals, lovingly prepared by Karen and her crew. Organic and locally sourced as much as possible, with a lot coming from Tolhurst Organic on the estate. Food as medicine: it supports your yoga and meditation.

Please tell us about allergies when you book.

q: Who is the teacher?
k: teacher dmitry dima who are you about karen sadhama
a:
I'm Dmitry Glazkov. I teach vipassana in the Mahasi Sayadaw tradition, plus yoga and Ayurveda. I sit a month-long or 21-day retreat myself every year, and I teach at the Indriya Retreat Centre on Koh Phangan in Thailand, as well as here at Hardwick.

Karen Buckland, my wife, runs Sadhama with me and cooks the food. I'm not a guru. In the Dhamma, I'm more like a friend who has walked a few steps ahead, helping you with yours.

q: Do you run retreats in Thailand?
k: thailand koh phangan indriya abroad january
a: Yes. I teach Insight Vipassana at the Indriya Retreat Centre on Koh Phangan, Thailand. The next one is 25–31 January 2027: seven days, the same noting practice, by the sea. From $350, with a $100 deposit. You can book it on the retreats page.

q: How many retreats until I get results?
k: breakthrough progress results how long until
a:
It's gradual. Some people have a breakthrough on their first retreat. Most on their third. Some later down the line.

Don't measure it like that. Can you play Rachmaninoff after two days? No. But everyone can do it with faith and energy, given a full go. Does it help you be a better member of your family, your society? Then it's working.

q: What should I read to support my practice?
k: books read suttas recommend reading study
a:
The original teachings. The Buddha's own words, the Pāḷi Canon. If you don't study the diamond itself, how will you know what a diamond is?

Start with the Dhammapada, a few verses a day. Then the Satipaṭṭhāna Saṁyutta, and short suttas from the Aṅguttara Nikāya. All are in our free library. You can read online, download, or press Listen.

q: Do I have to be Buddhist?
k: buddhist religion belief christian spiritual faith convert
a:
No. Vipassana comes from the Satipaṭṭhāna, a teaching of the Buddha, but it doesn't require any belief system. It's a universal technique of observation. People of any religion, or none, practise it without conflict.

Nobody will try to convert you. You'll just see for yourself how it works. And faith comes naturally when you see it working.

q: Why meditate in nature?
k: nature outdoors forest trees why nature entrainment
a:
Entrainment. We fall into the rhythm of where we are. Two pendulums, out of sync, next to each other overnight: by morning, in sync. Fifteen minutes at Bank station and you take its tempo. A week by the river under the oaks, and the mind slows to the pace of the trees.

The Buddha practised in forests and groves. What we breathe out, the tree breathes in.
